extracted.intended_audience: conference organizers, program chairs, area chairs, reviewers, and researchers interested in peer-review process design
extracted.subtask_description: Summaries and actionable insights from randomized experiments run on ICML 2020 testing resubmission-disclosure effects, discussion-management/herding, and novice-reviewer recruitment/mentoring to evaluate and improve conference peer-review processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission Bias (disclosure of prior submissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do reviewers get biased when they know that the paper they are reviewing was previously rejected from a similar venue? (Experiment: telling reviewers before reading that the paper is a resubmission.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key finding: reviewers give almost one point lower score (95% CI: [0.24, 1.30]) on a 10‑point Likert item for overall evaluation when told a paper is a resubmission; 'Paper Quality' is underrated the most. Implication: conference organizers should evaluate the trade-off between reducing resubmissions and introducing unfairness. One concrete mitigation: postpone revealing the resubmission signal until after initial reviews are submitted. Also account for this effect when deciding whether to make reviews public (e.g., on OpenReview).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall evaluation (10-point Likert) as a measurement metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall evaluation of a paper measured on a 10‑point Likert item was used as the primary reviewer score metric in the resubmission experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aggregate score is sensitive to procedural signals (e.g., disclosure of resubmission history). Use caution interpreting changes in this metric when process changes (like disclosure timing) are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper Quality (review sub-criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrower review criterion—'Paper Quality'—used in reviews and specifically observed to be most affected (underrated) when reviewers are told a paper is a resubmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When auditing reviewer behavior or changing submission-history policies, examine sub-criteria (like Paper Quality) in addition to overall scores, since some dimensions may be disproportionately affected by biasing signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Herding in reviewer discussions (order effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditioned on a set of reviewers who actively participate in a discussion, does the final decision depend on the order in which reviewers join the discussion? (Experiment: randomized 'Positive Group' vs 'Negative Group' where the most positive or most negative reviewer was asked to start the discussion.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key finding: analysis of ~1,500 papers found no statistically significant difference in acceptance rates between groups — no evidence of herding in the discussion phase. Implication: discussion-management need not implement special countermeasures against herding during reviewer discussions, given these results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance rate as an outcome metric for discussion interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance rate of papers was used as the primary outcome to detect whether discussion-management strategies (order of contributors) produced systematic differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating discussion-management or other procedural interventions, measure downstream outcomes (acceptance rate) and test for statistical significance across randomized groups to detect practical effects like herding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novice reviewer recruitment via selection from auxiliary review performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Can researchers with limited/no publication history be recruited and guided to enlarge the reviewer pool without compromising quality? (Procedure: evaluate junior reviewers in an auxiliary process, invite the strongest 52 to join ICML as 'experimental' reviewers.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection based on demonstrated review quality (from an auxiliary review exercise) can identify novice reviewers who perform comparably or better than the conventional pool. When recruiting novices, use an evaluative selection step rather than purely affiliation/publication heuristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentoring/support for novice reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide experimental (novice) reviewers with a senior researcher as a point of contact who offers additional mentoring during their participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key finding: the combination of selection + mentoring yielded reviews rated at least as good as the conventional pool, with 30% of experimental reviewers' reviews exceeding expectations vs 14% in the main pool. Recommendation: pair novice reviewers with senior mentors to maintain or improve review quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review quality as rated by area chairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Area chairs' ratings of review quality were used as a principal metric to compare experimental novice reviewers and the conventional reviewer pool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use meta-ratings (area chairs' evaluations) to assess review usefulness/quality; report proportions exceeding expectations and comparable statistics when comparing pools or interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical oversight for running experiments on peer-review participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments involving reviewers were evaluated by an Institutional Review Board (IRB); the IRB approved conducting the herding experiment without notifying participants because awareness could obscure findings and risks were judged minimal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When running randomized experiments that affect reviewers/authors, obtain IRB or equivalent ethical review, carefully assess risks, and document justification for (non-)notification of participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design/sample representativeness and confounder control
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental choices (e.g., selecting junior reviewers primarily from US schools and keeping the call non-public) affect generalizability and may introduce affiliation confounders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations: small, convenience samples (US-based junior researchers) may not generalize. Mitigation: compare experimental reviewers to conventional reviewers from the same institutions to address affiliation confounding; consider broader sampling or replication at larger scale before generalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy trade-off evaluation (procedural changes vs fairness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes like requiring authors to declare previous submission history may reduce reviewer load but can introduce unfairness via bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conference organizers should explicitly evaluate trade-offs when adopting procedural rules: quantify anticipated operational benefits (e.g., reduced resubmissions) against measured harms (e.g., score reductions due to bias), and consider process modifications (timing of disclosure) to mitigate harms.
